blocks.x: The End The End Okay, I'm going to get the date. 31st of January 1962, Eddie Dawson, Type 1. Can you tell us your birth date, Eddie? When were you born? 19...let me see...24th of July. 24th of July. What year would that be? That was...1884. Uh huh. And did any of your family play instruments before you? No, no. Did you pick it up? Just picked it up myself. How old were you when you first started playing? About 18. You bought yourself a bass, did you, or did you make one up, Paul? Uh huh. You bought a bass from a store? I bought a tenor banjo from... Oh, you started on tenor banjo. And then a guitar. Uh huh. That was about... That was around...I was about 18 then. Yeah. Uh huh. Um, where did you get the idea you wanted to be a musician? Just, uh... Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

So I'll tell you why, they fired Billy Moran for me. Took me in the band, they had a falling out. Which band was that? That was that band they had to call it the... I don't see that band. Whose band was it? Who was the leader? Yeah. Wait now. Billy Moran and let me see who's the leader now. How you call him? He's a trumpet player. Good trumpet player too. Perez was it? Manny Perez. Manny Perez. Manny Perez. Who else was in that band? Do you remember that Eddie? Oh man, that's been Manny Perez, Billy Moran and George Beckhead. I think one of them boys we was just now talking about. Yeah, he was playing guitar. John Moran? John Moran? Yeah, he was playing guitar. John Moran? Yeah, he was playing guitar. John Moran? Yeah, he was playing guitar. Yeah, on drums. Remember that? No, let's see. I really can't think of who he had on drunk. When was it you played with Paris? You know, I just played while, you see. After Hifalight Charles Band or before? Yeah. Oh, after that. After that. Yeah. I didn't play with them long because they had a, after they had, they was playing spot jobs, you see. Most of their jobs were just like I say, out at the Karellas, out to the lake. Did Paris play mute it or did he play open horn? Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. just like them guys down there on the 135th in the house. I mean, in Harlem, down there, on the 135th, 34th, 32nd, all out there on the sidewalk in the pool hall with them old box bags. You're out of style, you're out of date, boy. I said, what are you talking about, man? I said, he's made in great big letters. E-B-G, my initial, you're dope. He said, listen, the goods are fine. I'm not criticizing the goods, but the style, you're out of style they would wear. That's when pinch bags first come out. Little belt in the back, you know, pinch bags. That's what they call the pinch bags. Yeah. I said, man, you don't think I'm going to be wearing that thing? He says, man, well, sure, you're just not used to wearing these old long coats, look like an overcoat, are you? Them big old bulldog shoes. I said, you're out of style, you're a professional man now. You want to get in line. I said, all right, I'm going to show you this evening. So he came along, we got to see them. He said, come on, let's stand out by the stage entrance. I was standing out there, long come one of these juggers, you know, old spray boy. And he didn't look hot, but he was all Englished up, you see?
Yeah.

And he come in, he had kid gloves on, a walking cane, spats, you know, and he had a beautiful brown suit on, a nice brown hat split down the middle, you know. He said, now look at that. See that? Don't he look all right? That's the way he was. I said, man, but he used to them kind of clothes I used to want. He said, but just look at yourself and look at that man.
For the peg, what do you call them?
Peg tops.
The pants, that is part of the outfit, but the back, the box.

Yeah, box bags, you see, and the coat come way down almost to your knees. I don't remember exactly what the box bags were. So he says, all right, finally here come a couple more fellas, man and his wife, you know. There you are. So look at them, how they look. Don't they look nice? Well, they did look all right, but I couldn't stand that pink bag. I said, man, I don't know. Wouldn't that look funny on me? He said, that's what you think. He said, you look funny with this suit on, but you don't know it. You're not in style. Oh, the next day, he goes out. I was out and I come in and I heard somebody say, yeah, he come now. And when I come through the hall, I go to the dressing room, I go, yeah, he come now. Oh, look what's up, oh, what's happening? Come here, Garland. Come here. And I went in there. And there was a boy, Eugene Colliner, the drummer. He was trying to fit this suit on him, you know. This coat and the sleeves come way up here. And the man said, this suit ain't for nobody. I don't want nobody to have this suit but that little baseball. Come here, Garland. Try this on. I said, hold on. And this fellow come and say, try that coat on. Go ahead now. I'll pull off my old long coat and I put the coat on. It looked like it was made for me. Sleeves come right through there, you know, put it on. Of course, it looked funny with the old peg tops, you see, and it was out like that. He says, go in the dressing room and put off your trousers and put on these trousers. I put on the trousers, honestly, it was the same as in the tail hat made the suit for me. And it didn't look good. And I kind of liked it. It looked in the glass, you know, in the dressing room. It got glasses all around. I said, this did look good. Well, the same spoiler was the big shoes. So I come out and he said, no, you see the difference? I said, yeah, I sure do. I tell you what I do. He said, this is a brand new suit. He says, I'm going on my vacation after this show, after this week. You wear this suit and I'll let you have this suit for $12. He says, I'll pay $75 for this suit. I'll let you have this suit for $12 if you promise you'll wear it in box pack. I said, all right. I'll pay. I said, wait up. I saw it in my pocket, my pants. I said, no, don't pay me now. I said, you wait till payday. The last show you get paid. He said, no, you keep your money. You may have to get something else. Now they're framing to make me get shoes and hats now.
Oh, yeah.

See? I put on a guy like that. And the girl says, you look like a gentleman now. That's what you need. All right. So the kid said, well, after the show tomorrow, now this is the next day now. He says, we're going out. Why don't you go with me? All right. I goes on out with the kid. And the first thing we got ready to go, Florence called me. He said, what's your father's address? I said, why? He said, well, you know, when you go abroad, you know, we got to have a dress case and things happened.
Yeah.

He used to go to Honolulu, see. Then going to Europe. I said, well, ain't you got that? He said, no, I don't remember having it. We ain't got it in the book yet. He ain't never looked for it, you know. I said, 2538 Cleveland Avenue. Uh-huh. He said, there's a foster call. Oh, he said, yeah. Well, that's all right. He said, come on, let's go. All right. We went on off. He's taking me down somewhere downtown. It was in Rock Island now. He's taking me downtown and brought the first place he came to me was to the shoe store. Hammond shoe store. One of the nanny wanted to see a pair of tan shoes, brown shoes. And they come out, you know, English shoes, you know, kind of pointed. I said, man, I don't want the more pointed to sharp toe shoes. He said, listen, fella, you're English, no? You got to get shoes to match your suits. You don't want these big old box toe shoes. You got a pair of English shoes and put them on off the door. They fit me good. Well, it must have been twelve or thirteen dollars, I think. I think. I said, no, we're going right up here. And they went to Meyer's hat company. Went in there and he wanted a brown hat. And I thought he was going to get a brown hat for himself. I said, you, what you getting a hat? He said, yeah, I'm going to get a hat. I said, what's your size? He said, I got no hats, man. He said, but what's your size? Seven. He said, bring me a seven hat. I said, you think I'm going to wear that thing split down the middle? I said, yeah. I got a seven hat and put them on. It looked nice in it. I'm taking that. Then he goes over the shirt place and he buys three shirts, three nice old shirts. I had some shirts on the barber pole, as you call them, barber pole. Oh, yeah.
Strikes over as almost as big as this chair. I had great big. I've seen a couple of guys.

Yeah. I said, all of those stuff you got in. You got all the lines. I'm getting you clean away from that kind of stuff. See, and them old rounders wear those. See, I don't wear that stuff no more. They bought me three shirts. He said, now next week, say, there you get more and more. Then you get your suit, order your suit. See?
Yeah, take all your pay when that's going on.

I had me town to the theater and I come back there, bundle all the little, little bundle, and the girls, all they did was going on. Walks in the theater and walks in the theater and, what's it got going with? What's it got going with? What's it got going with? It's your baby, you know. I went out there and framed it. Turned it loose and got all these shirts. So they says, go and here's your receipt for it. Receipt for what? From the American Express. I said, something come here for me? He said, no, you sent something. I said, I ain't sent nothing. Sure, we sent all your clothes to your daddy. They sent everything I had. They picked all your old clothes? Picked all them old box bags but the one I had on. Hats and I had two pair of shoes there and one pair I had on, that was all. Everything, all them old shirts, and I had quite a few. But there was no big old Bible post shirts. They sent all that away. And I had to start all out new. So, oh, that show, that evening when they got ready, they go that morning. They first show, and I come back down there, I was all dressed up. The kids see that I dressed up because I was right there with him. He dressed me up and I come down there, even to all white performers. I said, is that the bass player? I said, that's him. I said, I didn't look hot, you know. And so, I come in. He said, now I tell you what I'm going to do. We was in Peeler, Illinois. I said, we'll run down to Chicago when we get off tonight. We got off and went down to Chicago, you know, get there. It was all before one o'clock. I walked in the Deluxe and everybody run up all entertaining. I said, now you look like a gentleman. I said, what you mean? You got all those little box backs off. Everybody come home and kiss me.
They really were out of style then.
I was out of style, box backs, sure.
Had they worn those old box backs all over the country?
All over the country, but you understand the professional people didn't wear that kind of junk. That kind of junk was for old hustlers, you know. Yeah, like John New Orleans.
Yeah.

That's where the old hustlers were and all that stuff. But the professional man, you know, he was all together different. So, when I got there, everybody got to compliment me in the deluxe, you know, and all. Well, I got feeling good then, you know. I didn't look good. Oh, yeah. That'd be better. So, finally when I was there, when we hit to Chicago, I went right away and ordered me two suits of clothes made. Made. Didn't want to buy them already. We had them made. Made me two suits. That's how I started out. But I was funny. They had to take my clothes away from me. And I was out of line, but I wouldn't go for it. And the trombone player, he had some box bags. He had them somewhere and had them cut down.
For real?
But I said, I ain't going to have mine like that then. I said, I ain't got nothing to cut out, no. He didn't send all my clothes away. Even to my overcoat and all.
Well, I was going to ask you, when you mentioned about playing, did they, in the old days in New Orleans, did they have different uniforms? Seems like somebody called them.
Yeah. Yeah, well, that's the way it is. We got military uniforms.
Somebody talked about the boys in blue. Which band was that? Maybe Johnny St. Cyr was telling me. Wasn't it the boys in brown?
Well, I was trying to introduce them. And there's Eagle Band. Eagle Band had brown uniforms. We had a revelation blue uniform.
The Ori Band.
Just like the Imperial Band had.
The Imperial had blues.
They had blues too.
And that's the Ori Band that you had?
We had blue ones with Ori. Ori's Band on it. Ori's Band. Did you have caps?
Yeah. For the dance, not the brass band, but inside too.
That was for the orchestra. We had caps, oris. Just like the brass band. Like a military uniform.
Did they wear those caps inside too? Yeah.
Yeah.
Did they dress up that way?
We got our uniforms, yeah.
Yeah, I forget about those. Nowadays they never have any special.

No, nowadays. Now, lately you wear, we used to wear it. We had different suits. We had gray. And we had some kind of a light brown uniform. We'd buy a suit. It was up to us. Well, it was up to me. I used to be the one in charge of all that. Picking out the suits, you know. We'd have them made, you know. We'd wear clothes, you see.
Yeah, I was wondering about those.

Yeah, we used to wear uniforms. Military uniforms. And we got to Chicago, we had brown there. Lil had her one made. Oh, even places like the Greenland and all that? Yeah, Lil, she had her one made. She wore a uniform, kept and everything just like us.
I never knew that.
I never saw it. Yeah.
I was going to ask about any of the other old halls that you played in. You mentioned that Come Clean Hall, was it? Over in...
That's over in Dretton. Mm-hmm.
And other places that Ory might have played when he was... When you first joined him.

Well, I'd say, when I first joined him, we used to play quite a bit for long parties, you know. Private affairs. And played lots of time out to West Stand and out to Millenburg, you know. Oh yeah, those camps. Camps, you know, Sundays, you know, those different clubs, you know. They'd have their... Go out there at 9 o'clock in the morning, stay till 6 o'clock, you understand. Then come right on in and go down to Economy Hall. Yeah. Play till 4 o'clock in the morning. Leave home 9 o'clock, then get back home, hold at 2, 3 o'clock. I mean, 5, 6 o'clock in the morning.
Yeah.
Cause you play at 4 o'clock, you know, those dances down there all night long.
Uh... I was gonna ask a little bit more about any other bass players. Do you remember old man Glenny Albert?
Albert Glenny? Yeah, I remember Glenny.
Which bands?
That was one of the old timers. He just died this year, you know.
He was 88 years old when he died. What? 88, uh-huh.
Well, I'll be doggone, yeah.
He was considered about the oldest musician there. He sold his bass about 2 years ago, but until he was about 86, he still had his bass.
Well, I'll be doggone.
He still played jobs.
Hmm. Well, he was older than, uh... Uh... Uh... What do you mean? What am I trying to call? Slowdrag? Oh, Slowdrag. Oh, yeah.
He's a lot older than Slowdrag. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I know that old man. Slowdrag's just about, oh, something like 70 this year, I think. I'll be doggone.
The Glenny was 18 years older, yeah.
Whew. Well, there I remember, I can remember him good.
He had a full-size bass. He had a big bass. When I was a kid, I can remember that. I remember him good.
I think they say he used a three-string bass for years, but when I first met him, he was using four-string.

Well, later years, they all used a four-string bass. Yeah, they all used. They all used a four-string bass. I've got quite a few of them. I don't know who it could be, and I wouldn't know how to... Very few... Half, they know nothing at all. Can't sing a E-string now, make those pedal notes.
Yeah, well, they never used those much, I guess.
No.
Did you ever, when you used your bow, did you all re-hair the bows themselves? Somebody told me once about some... I was hiring with thread.
Yes. I used to take thread, number eight, black thread.
You did that job yourself then?
Myself, yeah.
The black thread.

Black thread. I used to take black thread, get a piece of thread, and nail along like that, you know. Would that be sort of the twist of thread? Around, no, just make it come just like that, just like, you know. Put them all together to get straight to that, boom. Then you tie it on each end. Yeah. Then you put it in. Then you get people, we used to take some hot rosin and put it on in there, you know, push it down in and take the rosin and light the matches. Melt it, you know, and put it down there, then turn it over, then put that little peg down in there. With rosin?
Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Put pieces of hot rosin down there. Lots of people used to get the switcher carmen and put on the, what do you call that stuff? It's rain. Oh yeah, ceiling wax. Ceiling wax.
Yeah, yeah.
I've seen them. Yeah, that's what generally put in there.
I reherded a violin bow last year, I put glue in there.

Yeah, well first, you know, put anything to hold it. You see, you can't get it out though. Yeah. And we put ceiling wax in there, that's what goes in there. We put rosin in there, or we break down, we didn't care, we put it on the side.
That thread would hold the rosin all the way.

I throw it in there, that thread would, and riled them up good, because I riled them and hung it on all the way they were done, all the way they were done, sure. Start, and pull right on. Lots of things. I've seen the time I went out in the country and string broke, a G-string broke, and I got one of them white piece of twine, size of a G-string.
Oh yeah.
A fella throw me out there in the holy home, in Laplace, if you get this piece of string, you can make a string out of that.
Yeah, I imagine you would get it.

And I put it on, tied it on there, tuned that thing up, and it went on up, sounded like a G-string. Just put a lot of rosin down there, you know, where the bulls go. And I said, can you beat that? I played the whole night long. Come on back into town with that string on there. I took it off, I wouldn't keep it off. They danced it.
Do you remember Danny Lewis? Danny Lewis?

I remember him well, that's my buddy. I used to pitch hit for him with the eagle. Yeah. He hit there, and Danny Lewis hit John and the Dots of the Island. We'd draw the pitch in there and say, we used to do what I always say, you see. Yeah. And we used to get behind them, you know, when they'd run, and say, da da da da da. Yeah. You know? So, what's that? Old Frankie Dukeson died, and old Danny Lewis cried. And Edward Barton put it aside. He could print good, he could draw good. He'd draw the side, and put all that on, and he held that wagon in there with Frankie's wagon, he hid it that way. You see? And we'd blowin', and you could see the sparks coming, the stars was coming out of Ores, come boom, you know, after Frankie Dukeson. You could see where they, they was running. And I went in time, put that sign at Pedida and Franklin, I mean Pedida and Rampart, right on the side, on Pedida Street side. There used to be a little wagon that way to sell shrimps, crabs, and stuff there. And I placed it right on the front, and I was putting the nails and tats in it. And I used to hang out with all them guys, and I wasn't afraid of them guys, you know. There were some tough ones there. And when I put them guys see that, we had the nails there, you know. Old Frankie Dukeson died, and old Danny Lewis cried. I was, catch him, do what he always said, and you could see him running. And man, them guys started to laugh, and they went in, they'd come out here and see something. And Danny Lewis was in there playing poonga. He didn't like it. Man, they'd run out there and see that. Now here comes Johnny Dukeson, and after I put it on, Johnny Dukeson came down there. He was looking at the front, started laughing. And Johnny Dukeson, we laughed so hard, you know. Quah, quah, quah. Danny Lewis called, ooh, so-and-so put that up there. And this boy, Johnny Dukeson, quah, quah, quah, quah. Quah, quah, quah. He said, you put that up there? He said, no. Quah, quah. I said, I'll put it up there. He said, well, he wasn't going to do me. He wasn't going to hit me. No, he wasn't going to hit me. I was as tough as they were, too. Yeah. Yeah, he wasn't going to hit me. And I was pretty good with him. I said, I'll put it up there. He was playing with Frankie Dukeson.
He was playing with Frankie Dukeson.

Yeah, he was a bass player. Yeah, I said, I'll do it up there. What? He said to Johnny, what are you laughing at? I said, quah, quah. I went to Johnny and said, quah, quah, quah. Man, he hauled off and hit Johnny in the eye. Boom. He was playing with Johnny in the eye. And Johnny had his uniform on, too, you know. Yeah. But he didn't have his clarinet because he was left down the street at Miss Martin's. That's where we always meet. We're going to play a funeral. Hit Johnny in the eye. I said, I'll laugh. Ha, ha.
I see.

Man, I'll laugh like that. Johnny went back and I was always hanging out. Then we went back to Miss Martin and said, what's the matter with you? He said, Dan Lewis, I said, Dan Lewis hit him in the eye.
Yeah.

He was down there. I said, Dan Lewis hit him because he was laughing at me putting that sign up there. Why didn't he hit you? I said, it got thin, so he ain't going to hit me. He better not hit me. He didn't shine him because he was there. So, Miss Martin got a stick. She went by and said, here's my good stick I got for dinner. Put this on your eye. He said, put the whole stick across down his eye. Oh, gee. Johnny said, well, keep that up there to play in the funeral. Well, you can keep that up there until you get ready to leave. We got up there, kind of dry it down a little bit and she had some dark glasses. They give them dark glasses. Now, all the way we go to the old play in the funeral, they say, oh Johnny Dots laugh, Dan Lewis bust him in the eye. I thought he was concerned with more things, you know.
Yeah, yeah.

Hey there too, there's one. What did Dan Lewis do? I said, whopped him in the eye. I bet Johnny was mad. Oh, Johnny, he'd be like, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. He said, come on there. And this was a good way to say something to him. He said, did he hit him hard? I said, did he? I said, look at his eye. And as soon as Johnny Dots started to say something, he said, ta-da. You know, they're ready to play, you know. Well, they go out and laugh at you, don't care what happens. They stand up there and fall down and they laugh. Get up from there. Yeah, you fall down, get up from there. The bass fell off my back and the neck come off. They just laugh. Oh, Lord.
And at the funeral you played, what did you play drums?
I played, no. I played drums too, but I played alto horn. Or alto horn.
Peck horn.

We used to say peck horn. Yeah, it was a round one. No, not a mellow one. Peck horn. Straight up there. Straight up there. Straight up there. Yeah, straight up there. You didn't have laughter beats. That, that, da-da-da-da-da. I used to play peck horn. About the same as the snare drum part.
The guitar player, he played.
He played, he played good, a mellow phone player. He played mellow phone too, huh? He was a pretty good alto player, yeah. Who played bass drum in that? I guess Henry Martin played snare drum.
No, snare drum.

I used to play bass drum most of the time, but when we were in the big band up, I'd play alto. Finally, I got, we used to let Black Benny play bass drum. Yeah. You heard of him, didn't you? Oh, yes. Yeah.
Yeah. Right Benny was playing. Armstrong, this Armstrong's always talking about. Yeah.

It was one of his players. Yeah, it was. He used to fight for the band. He'd go out and fight for the band. Nobody wouldn't do us nothing. He used to take care of us. He was a tough one. He was tough too. He liked to fight. He loved to fight.

Well, I was going to ask you, we just have a couple more minutes on here, so if there's anything about the New Orleans style of playing that everybody talks about, the New Orleans style being different in other places in the country, like say when you went to Chicago and heard the other bands and…
Well, the style was in the rhythm. It's the rhythm. All right. Now, in Chicago, it was two beats. And we had the full beat. Yeah. See, Chicago. And I'll go… . . . . . Two beats, full beats we had.
The bass drum?
Bass drum, all right, full beats. One, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, all the way. And that'd be .
Yeah, the piano.
Yeah.
The low notes and then the high, like that.
That's correct. That was the difference.
Was there any difference much in the melody, the fact that they...
In playing the full beats? No.
In the New Orleans bands and the other bands? In the melody? In the variations or anything that they did or what would you say?
Well, no, no, we just took some tunes. The only thing we played would have different arrangements probably on a number, you know. No, it wouldn't be no difference.
I mean anything that was typical about the way they played the melodies in New Orleans, different than other places?

Probably we wouldn't play, you'd take some of the boys coming out of New Orleans and play some of those numbers. Probably they didn't play it correctly. They might probably leave out the middle part of a number, you know. You see, they probably didn't play but a chorus of it. Just over and over the chorus, you know. More simplified. That's right. They never played the beginning of a number, you know. Voice, somebody said, as far as they'd play a voice and play two chords, then we'd take the third strain and the following may play just a voice and a chorus. One of them boys from New Orleans, we'd just play choruses.
Yeah, they still do that a lot now.

Yeah, just play choruses, yeah. They don't even know the chorus. No, don't know it. Now you'd take those bands, we'd come back there, they'd play as is. This was on that sheet music. We'd come back there, we'd change that thing around. We'd play in that style. That's the difference between boys.
I wondered, did you ever work out any routines of playing, say, the first chorus loud or the introduction loud and then the next part soft?

Oh, yeah, yeah, oh yeah, yes. We shaded the music. That's one thing about that older band. That's why they used to call us the soft, they used to call us sweet, sweet and soft, something sweet. We used to play so soft. We'd start out 40 in the induction. And come on up and play chorus medium. Then we'd come down.
Real soft.
Let's hear their feet. That means because . Then we'd come up, we'd start and then we'd come up, you see.
And we'd down. All right, hold on.
That's shit our music. Yeah. Well that's one thing War II was good for. That's why we made a big hit right out here in California. Against the black and tan band.
I heard Mutt talk about that once too. I forget what he called it, soft sweet swing or something like that. I don't know how he expressed it.
We used to say, that's the other feet.
Ram told me that yesterday too.
Foot City.
Soft.

Yeah. He really used to do it too. He'd get out. They'd mute those horns, you know. And that's where your bass and your rhythm sticks out, you see. The rhythm sticks out. But not too much of them. They play that when you play it soft. And I'd be making the full beat. Boop-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum- Nobody could play the bass, I could play for Bud Scott. Bud Scott didn't think, you know. You're a solid bass player, you're solid. There's all these bass players in here, but you're solid. Bud gets hit that guitar and he'd look over there. He had a certain beat he'd hit and he'd know that's all I wanted to hear, and I was ready. I was kind of leaned down like, you know, and bust a jack-chick-chick-chick. Then I'd say, here's a little Bud of Grid, you know. You know he got me.

I was going to ask about the tempo, that is, some of the bands today I notice play things so fast, like the Saints go marching in and all. Would you say it's characteristic of New Orleans not to play things too fast, or what did you

say? Because we never know, we don't play nothing, we didn't play nothing like that fast. Now here, lately they got playing some playing pieces, I like when the Saints come marching in, they played so fast, you understand? Nobody couldn't dance, but they just played. Yeah, you couldn't do nothing. But they sat there and listened at them. No, we didn't play nothing like that. In fact it was a gallop, a gallop, you know. This whole style. No, we always played things you could march or dance part. We used to play, we'd start off. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da They're there where we shout, you know. We didn't play like these guys played. They're cleaning that fast.
Yeah, some of them today play everything so fast.

Everything is fast. I was like those bebop players. They play things, you don't know what they're playing because you don't know the melody. You can't hear no melody. There ain't no melody. They're just running a scale. Turn the saxophone and take it and he runs with 24 bars. Nothing but a scale. Then the next man he take it. What you playing? I don't know. He just played. They played South Ramport Street Parade one day. One night I played with them and never knew what I was playing until way after the thing was over. I asked him what was we playing? He said South Ramport Street Parade. Oh yeah, I couldn't take the name of it. Never knew what I was playing.
Did they use as many solos in the old days in New Orleans or more ensemble?

Well, they use more solos now, but in the old days we didn't use the solos as much as we're using now. Yeah. Because I know we played some, I played a lot of solos on my bass violin, you know. Yeah. We didn't do that, you know. But we didn't do much of that. All we done was just give the horns and taking all that, taking everything, the horns, you know.
Would they take turns about or did usually when the trumpet or they say the clarinet took a chorus, did the trumpet come back of them?
Yeah. The chorus, yeah, yeah, yeah. They take a chorus. It's clarinet, you know. Yeah. And then in the background with trumpet and trombone, you understand.
Would the horns put down or would they play back?
No, they'd give them background, you understand. And some of them, they didn't give them some pieces, they'd rest. They'd play nothing. Sometimes they would dig around.
Yeah, yeah.

Just the rhythm was still going all the time. Yeah, whatever. Yeah. And the trumpet would pick it up, then the trombone would pick it up. Yeah. Yeah. But now, you see, lots of time now, we get the background now, you understand. And sometimes the clarinet player would pick it up and we didn't have to put the clarinet in the rhythm.
Yeah. Yeah, I understand. I just wanted to get you to express that, how the organ was. How the old band sounded, because I wasn't there in those old days to know just what they did. No.

It was much different than it is today. Most of the time we'd play a number right on the suit. You know the old way back, you know. Just go right on. Just play that number on the suit. The fellas pull it down and take a little rest and pick it right up again, you know. Chomp it, pull it down, where the clarinet and trombone have it, you understand. I would get a chance to rest a couple of bars.

You know, I think that's about all I wanted to ask you today. I don't like to take up a lot of your time, but I appreciated hearing this. I know a lot of people will. This is Rio 3, Eddie Dawson, January the 31st, 1962. You want to sit here and watch the machine Barry? That'll make it easier for me. Sure. And the donut's going to come. We've got minus one mark on top, you see. Okay. Let's see. Can we get your name on here again? Yeah. Your full name, I never did get that. Eddie Dawson. That's your full name? Yeah. No middle name? No.
Joseph. Joseph, huh? Edward Joseph, Eddie Joseph.
And you mentioned some guys gave you a nickname, huh?
Who were they? Yeah, Alphonse Peek Good and Javala. Where was it? That was down at Miller Phillips. I mean at Hunts and Nagels.
And what did they call you? They called me a rat.

Well, I'll tell you why, you know. We used to have to pass the hat around, you see. Mm-hmm. Pick up tips. And I'd run around with the hat, you know, and come back. And I was so fast, you know, that's when they started to call me a rat. And they started to call me a rat then. From that on, all the musicians, practically every one of them, most of them. Old ones, all of them knowed me about rats.
And who was the clarinet by that? You said it was Piku then, huh?
Alphonse Peek Good, yeah. He played with the... Was there another one there? No.
Any other clarinet player of them?
No. No, just Peek Good and Eddie Atkins was playing trombone, you know, I think. That's been a long time. Eddie Atkins and Piku. That was the Magnolia Band.
Mm-hmm. I thought you said there was a little dog fellow there on clarinet at one time.

Well, he did have me meet you. He's dead now. I'm trying to think his name off. Y'all know him good, too. He died up in a parish somewhere up in France. You mean Sidney Bichet? Sidney Bichet. Sidney Bichet.
And you said he was about to bash tail on there earlier.

Yes, indeed. He was playing with... You see them bands, that time, you know, they'd have a little fallin' out with a fallin' like that. They'd get another fallin', you know. They'd have a regular man. They all do the same thing. They'd have a regular man and if they have some kind of a little grievance with that man, then when you look around, he either quits or they're five and they'd get another fallin' and he'd stay with them a while and then... That's the way it was. You couldn't just keep... study men all the time. They used to have a little... just a misunderstanding between, you know. And if you're gettin' bad with the leader, well then you know what the consequence is. He'd serve to make it so miserable for you that you'd have to quit before he'd fire.
You know, I used to go uptown to a place called... Thomas Beer Garden in 1945 and saw a bass player up there named Tom Harris. Remember that?

Yeah, Tom Harris. Yeah, Tom Harris. Well, he wasn't much. He wasn't that... I think that's the same bass that I've got now. It was brand new and he had been working out of Lincoln Beach. And the lady out there that was running Lincoln Beach, she stood for security for that bass. He bought that bass from White Island. It was brand new. And I don't believe he had it two years when he died, you see. After he died, then I bought it. His aunt.
Who was he playing out at Lincoln Beach with?
Nah, he got me. He had a band out there. I can't remember, but he had a pretty fair band out there. But he was playing with that band. I don't know who...
I know he used to play with Avery and Tillman uptown when I heard him up by the park. Yeah.

At Tom Harris. Well, I guess that's about the same ones, you know. He had a band... That band was operating from Colton. That's the band that was way up in Colton. And he got that job out of Lincoln Beach. And that's a good bass. It's brand new. When I got it... He hadn't used it two years. You like new basses better than old basses? Oh, yeah. I can... I don't know. I like a new instrument. I used to have an old bass. It was called... Maple. It was a pure maple bass. And I used that bass and patched it up in cracks, you know. It'd get cracks in it and have it patched up and sealed in cracks up. And I used that bass a long time before I got this bass. I've been having this one for years now. After I got that cable, I took care of it, you see. I was very careful with it. I had an old bass that I used to use on advertising. You know, a long time ago bands used to go around and advertise, you see. On furniture wagons, you call it. Bands would get out and make advertising. And the trombone and the bass would be right on the tailgate, you see. Right on the back. And we'd stop on from corners, different corners like that. Sometimes we'd have a buck, you see. The kid ran in, run up on. Buddy Puthiel, Kid Punch, some of them. And Kid Punch was in his prime and he had a good band, too, you see. We all have a, what's it called, a buck. And then these kids and things used to run, people used to run around and follow them, their bands, when they advertised. See, like they're gonna have a dance at some club or another, some place or another. The day before that, that dance, they'd advertise for it. That's the way they used to do that. Track level, a little bit of Dixieland numbers. You can't shake, you can't shake like that. Sister Kate and all that, you know, Dixieland numbers. Hot numbers.
I wonder about that. What bands did you play with when you'd be advertising?

Well, it's like I said, I played, when I was playing, I was, when I played with Rene, that's practically most every, every dance he played for outside, dances he had to advertise. People hire, when they hire a band, they hire for the advertising, too, you see. They give you two dollars extra for that advertising. Did Rene ever buck against Louis Armstrong? Oh, Armstrong, practically yes. Well, Armstrong, he didn't, he didn't, didn't much, he didn't do much advertising. Uh-huh. You know, because when Armstrong came out of Jones' home, he, uh, he, uh, he started at, uh, Joe Segretta. Right up here on Liberty and Pedida. Uh-huh. But he started a little fish fries, he called fish fries, and he was playing a little, uh, say a trio, a piano, trumpet, and drum, clarinet. Uh-huh. And, uh, uh, Joe Segretta was running, running that fish fries at Liberty and Pedida. Well, then he had a little brass trumpet. They say trumpet is a cornet. A little sharp one, you know, what he came out of Jones' home with. And after he started, uh, going by Maurice, uh, got good with Guellarine and got, then got him a real trumpet. And, uh, he, he, first he started a six-piece band. Well, I played with him a good little while, too, you see, with, uh, Louis Armstrong. We played the first job, I know, to play a heavy job, was at the Junk Hotel, when we was wearing uniform, them, you know, like them, uh, uh, regular, uh, heavy coats, you know? Band coats with the high collars. Like the market band. Yeah, like, with caps. Uh-huh. And then heavy coats. Like the Imperial.
Yeah, like, yeah.

Well, uh, they'd have six pieces. We went to the Junk Hotel and played there. Well, he had Son Thomas playing guitar. I was playing bass. He had, uh, Dominic Remy on the trumpet. They had two trumpets. He had T-Boy Remy with him. And he had a fella called Pill on the clarinet. He died. He had a little bow-legged fella called Pill. Well, after that, well, Louis played around spot jobs around different places. And then, that's when he went up the line. Joe Oliver got with Joe Oliver. And him and Joe Oliver formed a band with Chicago. And they worked together with two of them in the same band until they fell out. Then Louis went his way and got his own band. Joe Oliver had his until he died.
And, uh, did he have a trombone down here, Louis? Used the trombone much?

Well, uh, yes. I used to use trombone. He had, uh, uh, let's see. His fellow was supposed to be a good trombone player. Uh, Jack Carey played with him a while on the trombone. He was an old trombone player. And he had, uh, uh, a fella called Benny Raphael. That was a pre-old fella. He was a good trombone player. Benny Raphael. And, uh, that's all I know. Uh-huh. Most of them.
Did you have another guy named Louis Prevost? Prevost.
Yeah, I know Prevost. What happened to him?
I don't know what happened to him.

He went away from here. Long time ago. I think he died. He went, he went, he went, uh, he went away the same time Bunk went away. Bunk Johnson. When Bunk left here, Prevost left. And they went up the line somewhere in different places and stayed away a long time, you see.
What did Prevost play?
We played, uh, Clammer Red I think. Yeah.
What about, uh, Morris French? Did you have another?
Morris French was a trombone player too. Well, Morris French played with Kid René a while too. Mm-hmm. He played with René a while.
Were you in the band then?

I played, I was in the band when Morris French was playing Trombone with him. And, uh, when we had, uh, the time we made that time, uh, we had that accident, uh, on, uh, Dauphine and, say Rock I think. Dauphine, it was an Italian fella had, he had bought a truck and he didn't, he didn't know much about driving. Well, they had a car, a street car was running down Dauphine Street then. And when we got to, say, Rock and Dauphine, that's where the, uh, you bet with that accident he'd be frozen in the car, the truck on the track, and, uh, he didn't, he couldn't get the, the truck off the track quick enough for the car. The car came along and I jumped out the back of the, the truck. I hit my hip on the side, Morris French, he, he got his horn all busted. And René got his trumpet, uh, mashed, and my bassist got all grinded up in the, on the streetcar track. And, uh, so, well, René went and, uh, told me not to accept nothing, that he was gonna get a lawyer. And, uh, so I, same way, uh, I went to the public service and explained it to him and he showed me all the records and said, well, it's an interesting, and he faltered the driver, truck driver. And, uh, every, every seat of paper he turned over, the fella told me, he said, you know, I'm a old musician, fella at the public service. He said, now, he said, you valued your, uh, bass at $80, $85, that's what he said. Now, at that time on Ramport Street you could get second-handed basses, you see, had plenty of them. And he said, I know you can get a bass for $30 and a good one. So he said, uh, will you accept $30 for your bass? And I told him, yes, me. He gave me $30. Uh, René got sold with me, but I didn't care, but he, they wind up, none of them didn't get nothing for the answer, but he got all busted.
Except you, huh?

Yeah, me, I'm the only one who got $30. They got a lawyer and they tried to sue public service, and I knew they didn't have no chance, you know, with that public service. But I accepted the $30. And I went on Ramport Street and I got me old bass too. Cheaper than $30 too. I got a bass for $12. And I had that bass for a long time too.
What year was that?
Oh gee, that was way around, that was about, I think it was around 1910. That's around 1910 when I was with him.
Yeah. Before the big storm? Yeah.
Before that September storm. Yeah. Yes sir.
Who were you playing with when the September storm occurred?

Well I was practicing with Rene and then after the storm in 1915 I went to work, then I went to work at the Whitney Bank. After the crash came about and things got bad, you know, things got dull, so the law came up, I'd work, fight and go to jail. That was around 1917, you see. And so I just got tired of walking around. I just said, well I met a fellow over there and he was poor at the Whitney Bank and I asked him that he could have had an opening there for me and he said yes, he'd get me on on the night. And I went to work for the Whitney Bank in 1917 on September 12th. And I've been there ever since.
How long did you have to give up music?

Well I practically didn't give up music, I just kept on playing, you see. But I was, I'd get off at, see when I want to play at night like that, I'd ask the night man, the foreman, to let me off and I'd come back in the morning, you know, and after I'd get off my job and finish up my work, work late. So you could double-dip, huh? Yeah, I'd done that for a long time. Many times my bass was up in the corner in the Whitney Bank, coming off, right off the job, right on my regular jobs at the bank. See, I was doing cleaning up, I was doing poor to work at you. Now, well since I've been there so long, I've advanced up to a messenger now, and I don't have to do all that cleaning up. But at that time, that's all I was doing. We was playing. Night jobs, spot jobs, different places.
What about O'Neal Lavishay? Did you ever know him?

O'Neal Lavishay, well he was a violin player, I worked with him at a few clothes, it's been a little while. He died. He was a violin player. He worked for, he was, he worked for the post office too, he's a mail carrier. And he played violin, he played over at a few clothes, had a fella called a few clothes, had a nightclub just like Billy Phelps and all of them, right across from 25. 25's on this corner, right across from 25's. It was a little hall, he'd go through alley and go in the back, sort of a hall back there. Well he didn't have much of a band, he'd have about four or five pieces, something like that. He didn't have, he didn't have no trumpet, just violin, guitar, bass, and clarinet, something like that too.
You know, I never didn't understand about a few clothes that was built, would anybody come in from Basin Street?

Yeah, you could come in through the front entrance, you know, but the back entrance was on, on, on, you know, Basin Street was an alley like. It was an alley that you go, right from Basin Street, you could go through that alley and go right on into the hall and the ballroom was in the front, you see. It was a, it was a large size hall, you know, knocked it all about four to fifty people or something.
With white and colored in there from front?

No, no they didn't have it strictly white. They had tables, they had tables on the side, you know, for customers to sit down, you know, people come in and drink, you know. The women, they had women there hustling drinks for them, you know. And he was a big, big stout fella. He had, he was a big politician too. He had a good jerk in the city here. They call him Fuqua, George Fuqua.

What was a chop house? I always see that in old advertisements for the district. Chop house. Must have been a name for something else. Yeah, I don't know the chop house. Might have just been a restaurant.
Yeah, yeah.
They might have had hustling women there or something.
Yeah, that's right.
What about, O'Neal obviously, when did he die, do you know?
Oh, he been dead for a long time. I don't know exactly when he died in, but I know he been dead a long time.
Is that the same guy they call Skinny?
Not as I know of. You never did though? I never had no nickname as I know of. I always called him O'Neal average here, that's all.
Yeah. Did he work with menstrual shows, tent shows?
I don't think so. I don't remember.
Seems to me Gino told me about somebody. We can ask him about it. Uh-huh. Somebody with a similar name, maybe a relative or something. Do you remember Jip the Blood when they had that killing?
Oh, yes. That's, that's, that's, that's, uh, I didn't know much about him, but I, I remember the time, you know, when he, when he did do all that killing.
Well, what happened after the killing? Did things go on as normal or they closed down or what?
I think they did. Yeah, they closed down. They closed down? Yeah, that was, that was another bad killing.
Well, how many times did they close the district down?
Oh, often and on, you know, they let, let them run wild, you know, and then they close them down and they'd open up again, you see. That's the way they operated. Mm-hmm. Run wild, close them down.
Where were you playing when Jip the Blood killing was? Were you there in the district?
No, I wasn't. I wasn't. Mm-hmm.
Oh, I never did get straight. Uh, which instrument did you play first? Guitar, mandolin, or banjo?

Well, in fact, I'll tell you the truth, I believe I did start on the guitar first, but I, I, I, I, I played, I practically was playing both of them most at the same time, you see, because I could play guitar pretty good. Mm-hmm. And banjos, when they, a long time ago, the banjo came out behind the guitar. Mm-hmm. That's the way the banjos did, they come out behind the guitar. So I played guitar first, when, if you, if you, if you, if you do right, they say right, I play, I play the guitar first. Cause I remember now, the Italian fella there, uh, uh, on the corner of, uh, of, uh, of Bauer and Gravy, he was the one that sent off and got a little wonder for me, see, kind of banjo.
But when did you play mandolin?

Oh, I had been playing mandolin, uh, I think that's, uh, the same time I started playing guitar, picked up the mandolin too. Mm-hmm. Yeah, both, same time, when I went with Lonzo and whatever, you know, when I tell you, when I was going around serenading, I just started picking up mandolin like that, and got a hold of one, and, and, uh, somehow or another, this app like that, and got to, got to be a good mandolin player. And, uh, I could play anything I want on it. Just by here. If I could hear a number, I could hear a number, hear a, I'd take my mandolin and go on places.
Uh, uh, I wish you'd explain to me about the guitar style on those days. Did they play with a pick or with, same as thumb picks or flat pick? Yeah, use the pick.
Flat pick on guitar?
Yeah, flat pick, yeah. Would they ever use a knife playing on the guitar?

It's the only one they want to play, uh, say like they want to play like Spanish style, you know, they, they put a, uh, I call it a capotash, you know, a mute. Mm-hmm. And just take your knife and, you know, you could take your knife and, and, and, and play it like that on your lap, you see, and run your knife up and down the strings, you see. And then, some of them played that way.
Well, what would you tune it to in Spanish? To a chord then?
You'd really, you, you, in, in Spanish, in fact, you'd have to tune it, the whole instrument in Spanish. Mm-hmm.
It would be to a chord then?
Yes, it's like you tune it natural. You're only saying you change the tone of, uh, your G string, your H string, your, your G string, you know. Mm-hmm.
I see, so you, you had a, then if you strummed across it, when the bass came out, you'd have to tune it. You'd strummed across it, when that knife lady would be playing chords and everything.
Oh, yeah, you could, you could do, that, that knife would make them, you see.
Yeah. Just like, just like when you boss. Yeah, that's right. When you put one finger, the same kind of philosophy. Yeah, that's right.
Uh. Only thing, that would be all the strings you'd, you'd be pulling across, you see.
Yeah.
Uh-huh. I see. They were taught all right.
And so, but who would be playing the lead when you'd have two guitars? You'd say you had one Spanish and one natural tune.

Well, the, they wouldn't, neither one of them wouldn't be playing no lead. The, the violin would be playing the lead, but the, the guitar playing natural, he'd just playing compliments, you see. Mm-hmm. I see. And the other father would, with, with, with, with, uh, Spanish guitar, he would be playing the same way, you see. Mm-hmm. Playing compliments, but it would be two different tones, you see.
I see. Where's the battlefield?

Right across over here, it starts from, the battlefield starts from Galvis and, uh, at least from Claiborne and Perdita, takes in Perdita, Grabger, Perdita and Perdita, all the way back to Broad Street.
From Claiborne to Broad?

Yeah. It's from Claiborne all the way back, but it starts at Grabger. Mm-hmm. You got Grabger, you got Pedita and Perdita, that's straight there, the blocks. Now, I, then it goes all the way back to Broad, that's the battlefield.
And you lived around there?
Yeah, sure, I lived, I lived in a certain walk for, about, 25 or 30 years, I think.
Nice quiet neighborhood?

Yeah, that's, well, it was pretty bad a long time ago. It was pretty bad a long time ago. It was so quiet, I tell you. It was, they had some roughnecks around there, yes sir. The fellas was tough around there, policemen, you couldn't hardly get a policeman to go back there if something was happening. The detail of police, and that time unit, you'd have to beat police, you see, on the beat. The fellas used to ride a horse, police on a horse. As far as I see the time, Bradley took the police and took his gun and he clubbed him. Who's there? He had him under arrest, you know. And they were shooting dice and they had a corner called Mogul's Corner, right there, kind of a, uh, uh, uh, uh, Clara, Clara and uh, Cypress, didn't call it Cypress Street. Back there. I know. Back in the cemetery.
Yeah.

Now, the fellas used to shoot dice with candlelight, you know. And the police would slip upon them. Well, they broke and run, they'd break and run and all go. Some of them had that, had a, what's a couple of basins, that was a new basin out there. It was off, it wasn't filled in like it is now. But they'd run all around that new basin, they had a lumber yard back there, they'd get around that lumber yard. They'd run all around them different hours back there and behind that lumber, they couldn't find him. Well, they called Bradley. And the policeman had him. They grabbed him up and then, hasn't they had him up in the pants like that? You know, all right, he walked, when he walked, walked him till he could get to the telephone so he could ring up. Called away. Bradley took him side, stepped from him and cracked him and down he went. He took his gun and cloth and the hemorrheds. Used to wear them old big hemorrheds. Yeah, he was tough. The guys was bad back then in Battlefield.
Did you know Rabbit that played guitar?

Yeah, Rabbit, yeah, Rabbit, he was, he wasn't much, but he was used to sing a whole lot, you know. Fake, you know, go around and play around with fish fries, you see. There's a lot of fish fries. Every Saturday night, you see, you see all around Cypress Street. All them people used to get fish fries and hang a red lamp out on the front. The gateway, a red lamp. That was fish fries. People would go in there and sit down and eat fish and drink beer and stuff, you know. And they had the old drinks, they called it gin and raspberry. The gin and raspberry, you know, they put the raspberry syrup in it, make it pink. And wine, all that kind of stuff. And that Rabbit used to go around and play at them fish fries, you know. Mm-hmm. And he'd give them, just pay them a dollar and a quarter at night, that's all he'd get, a dollar and a half. But just sing and play.
What's your grandma called him Rabbit? Yeah.

The people would get in there and dance by his, just do the guitar, you see. Singing and playing the guitar, you know. He could sing to you, you know. And, uh, they'd be packed in the house, we'd be packed in the house party, you know. Fish fries, just like a house like this. Sometimes three rooms full of people. And people used to make money off their fish fries, too.
He made a good record, too, I tell you that. Yeah? I got a good record now. A rabbit?
Yeah. You see, you've been operating a long time, then. The rabbit's been dead a long time.
Well, I found the old record. Oh, I see.

segments.title: Dawson's birth date and first instruments
segments.summary: Dawson gives his birth date (24 July 1884) and says he taught himself, starting at about 18 on tenor banjo and guitar.

segments.title: Replacing Billy Moran in Manny Perez's band
segments.summary: Dawson says Billy Moran was fired and he took his place in Manny Perez's band; they recall who else played in it. The band mostly did spot jobs at the lake.

segments.title: Garland on being out of style: box bags and peg tops
segments.summary: Ed Garland, on a bundled recording, tells how a colleague mocked his old-fashioned box-back clothes and showed him a stylish English suit.

segments.title: Garland's new wardrobe: shoes, hat, shirts and Chicago
segments.summary: Garland describes being outfitted with shoes, hat and shirts, his old clothes being shipped home, and the praise he got in Chicago.

segments.title: Band uniforms in New Orleans: Ory's blues, Eagle brown, Imperial
segments.summary: Discussion of band uniforms: Eagle Band brown, Imperial and Ory's blue, caps, and Lil's uniform in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Garland: early Ory band and bass craft
segments.title: Early jobs with Ory: private parties, camps and Economy Hall
segments.summary: Garland describes what Ory's band played when he first joined: parties, Sunday camp outings and all-night dances.

segments.chapter: Garland: early Ory band and bass craft
segments.title: Old bassist Albert Glenny and three- and four-string basses
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about Albert Glenny, the oldest bass player, and they compare his basses and four-string bass use.

segments.chapter: Garland: early Ory band and bass craft
segments.title: Rehairing bows with thread and improvising a bass string
segments.summary: Garland explains rehairing a bow with black thread, rosin and ceiling wax, and tells of replacing a broken G-string with twine.

segments.chapter: Garland: early Ory band and bass craft
segments.title: Danny Lewis hits Johnny Dodds over a sign prank
segments.summary: A funny story about Danny Lewis, a sign Garland hung, and Johnny Dodds getting hit in the eye before a funeral.

segments.chapter: Garland: early Ory band and bass craft
segments.title: Brass-band funeral instruments and Black Benny
segments.summary: Garland says what he played in funeral bands (alto horn, bass drum) and recalls Black Benny as the band's tough protector.

segments.chapter: Garland on the New Orleans style
segments.title: New Orleans full-beat rhythm versus Chicago two-beat
segments.summary: Garland says New Orleans rhythm used four full beats against Chicago's two, and that New Orleans players changed arrangements.

segments.chapter: Garland on the New Orleans style
segments.title: Playing soft and sweet: shading the music and Bud Scott
segments.summary: Garland describes the old band's dynamics, the 'soft and sweet' reputation, and the rhythm he and Bud Scott kept.

segments.chapter: Garland on the New Orleans style
segments.title: Tempo of old bands versus fast modern playing and bebop
segments.summary: Garland criticizes fast tempos on tunes like the Saints and bebop for lacking melody.

segments.chapter: Garland on the New Orleans style
segments.title: Solos versus ensemble and background in the old bands
segments.summary: Garland explains how the old bands took choruses in turn with horns backing, and rhythm continuing.

segments.chapter: Garland on the New Orleans style
segments.title: Closing of the Garland recording
segments.summary: The interviewer thanks Garland and ends the session (the end of the text is garbled).

segments.title: Second tape: Dawson's full name
segments.summary: A new tape starts; the interviewer sets up the machine and confirms Dawson's full name as Edward Joseph.

segments.title: The nickname 'Rat' and the Magnolia Band
segments.summary: Dawson explains how passing the hat got him called Rat, names the Magnolia Band players, and recalls Bechet and bands' habit of changing men.

segments.title: Tom Harris and his bass
segments.summary: Dawson recalls bassist Tom Harris, who died soon after buying a new bass that Dawson later bought, and his Lincoln Beach band.

segments.title: Advertising on furniture wagons and Dixieland numbers
segments.summary: Dawson describes how bands advertised dances from wagons, his old maple bass, and Kid Punch.

segments.title: Playing with Louis Armstrong's first six-piece band
segments.summary: Dawson recounts Armstrong's start at fish fries, his first band at a hotel with Dawson on bass, and the trombonists he used.

segments.title: Louis Prevost, Bunk Johnson and Morris French
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Prevost leaving with Bunk Johnson, and Morris French playing trombone with Kid Rene.

segments.title: Streetcar accident with Rene's band and the $30 bass settlement
segments.summary: Dawson tells how a truck carrying Rene's band was hit by a streetcar and he alone accepted $30 for his smashed bass, around 1910.

segments.title: Leaving full-time music for the Whitney Bank
segments.summary: Dawson says he took a job at the Whitney Bank in 1917 and kept playing night jobs.

segments.title: O'Neal Lavishay and the Fuqua hall off Basin Street
segments.summary: Dawson recalls violinist O'Neal Lavishay and the nightclub hall run by George Fuqua, with the layout and clientele.

segments.title: The Jip the Blood killing and the district closings
segments.summary: They discuss the killing, and how the district was repeatedly closed and reopened; Dawson was not there.

segments.title: Learning guitar, banjo and mandolin
segments.summary: Dawson says he began on guitar, then banjo and mandolin, which he learned by ear while serenading.

segments.title: Spanish-style guitar played with a knife
segments.summary: Dawson explains Spanish tuning and playing the guitar with a knife, and how two guitars complemented the violin lead.

segments.title: The Battlefield neighborhood and its tough characters
segments.summary: Dawson describes the Battlefield area boundaries, living there for decades, and rough episodes with police and dice games.

segments.title: Rabbit and the Saturday-night fish fries
segments.summary: Dawson recalls guitarist Rabbit playing for small pay at fish fries, and the drinks and crowds there.

segments.title: Blues piano players who played alone
segments.summary: Dawson recalls a blind blues pianist and how solo pianists played limited keys and could not work with bands.

segments.title: District pianists and Dude Robertson
segments.summary: Names of district pianists such as Jackson, Cahill and Winenboy are given, and Dude Robertson, now a guitarist, comes up.

segments.title: Wrapping up the session
segments.summary: It is getting late; the interviewer says he wants to come back for more.
